561.title: Lucky to bear it
561.hook: not "I'm unlucky," but "I'm lucky to bear this without breaking" (Meditations 4.49)
561.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often apply the rule at the end of Meditations 4.49 to setbacks: the event is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the headland: it stands firm, and the water settles. Your line was spray flies up and falls back.

Listen to how people tell bad news. Just my luck. Why does this always happen to me? The sentence starts before we've decided what we think: a little reflex story about being the unlucky one. In the same entry as the headland, a few lines later, Marcus Aurelius catches himself in exactly that reflex, and rewrites the sentence. Same event. Different words. And the new words change what the event is.
screen: `JUST MY LUCK.` → `A REFLEX SENTENCE.` → `LUCKY TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Unlucky me, that this happened, Marcus imagines saying. Then he corrects himself. Not at all. Rather: lucky me, that though this happened, I'm still standing, not crushed by the present and not afraid of what's coming. Why call that luck? Something like this could have happened to anyone, he says, but not everyone would have come through it unbroken. So why call the event bad luck, rather than calling your steadiness good luck? Both are true; you choose the headline. Then a test. Does what happened stop you from being just, generous, self-controlled, sensible, careful in judgment, honest, modest, free? If it doesn't touch those, it hasn't touched what makes you who you are. And a rule for every future vexation: this is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune. This isn't pretending. Marcus doesn't call the loss a gain, or say it didn't hurt. He moves the word luck from the event, which you didn't choose, to the bearing, which is yours. The flat tire is a flat tire. Changing it calmly, on the shoulder, in the rain, without taking it out on anyone: that's the part that's yours, and it's a kind of luck to be able to.

562.title: The gulf of time
562.hook: look at the vast gulf of time behind you and ahead (Meditations 4.50)
562.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes take the view of Meditations 4.50 outdoors, looking at the night sky and measuring a worry against the vastness of time.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was good fortune, which lives in bearing a hard thing well. Your line was still standing, not crushed.

On a clear night, away from the streetlights, look up. Some of that light left its star centuries ago, long before anyone alive today was born. You're looking backward in time. Plenty of people feel two things at once out there: very small, and strangely calm. Marcus Aurelius had no telescope, but near the end of his fourth book he stands at the edge of the same view, and asks what it does to the length of one life.
screen: `A CLEAR NIGHT, NO STREETLIGHTS.` → `LIGHT OLDER THAN ANYONE ALIVE.` → `THE GULF OF TIME.`

segments.voice: He starts with what he calls an unphilosophical but still useful aid against the fear of death: think of the people who clung hard to life. What did they gain over those who died young? He names a few Romans who lived long and buried many others, and then were buried themselves. The gap between a short life and a long one, he says, is small. Then the view opens. Look at the vast gulf of time behind you, he writes, and the other boundless stretch ahead. In that infinity, what's the difference between someone who lives three days and someone who lives three generations? He seems to be playing on old Homer here: Nestor, the wise old king who outlived two generations of men and ruled among the third. Against the gulf, Nestor and an infant are almost the same size. Some people find that view frightening. The French writer Blaise Pascal, many centuries later, wrote, in Trotter's 1910 translation: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." Marcus finds something else in it: relief. If a life is a flicker in that dark either way, its length is not the thing to fight over. What matters is what you do inside your flicker. Both reactions are honest, and you may feel both on the same night.

563.title: Push it away
563.hook: how easy to push away a troubling thought and be at peace at once (Meditations 5.2)
563.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 5.2 with small, everyday troubling thoughts, noticing them and setting them down; serious grief or anxiety is met in other ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Nestor, almost the same size as an infant against the gulf of time. Your line was almost the same size. And book five begins.

Book five of the Meditations opens with Marcus arguing with himself in bed one morning, trying to get up. If you've ever hit snooze, you know that entry. The next one is shorter, and stranger. It claims you can push a troubling thought away and be at peace, right away. If you've ever lain awake replaying a conversation, you might laugh. Easy? But Marcus means something specific.
screen: `MARCUS IN BED, NOT GETTING UP.` → `A CLAIM THAT SOUNDS TOO EASY.` → `PUSH IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: How easy it is, Marcus writes, to push away and wipe out every impression that is troubling or out of place, and at once to be in perfect calm. The Greek word for that calm, galene, is the word for a sea gone flat after wind. What's he pushing? Not the event, not the facts. The impression: the first picture the mind paints, before you've agreed to it. Something happens, and an impression arrives saying this is terrible. You haven't yet said yes. The push happens in that gap. Why easy? The way putting down a cup is easy. The motion is small. What's hard is noticing you're holding it. Often we don't keep a troubling thought on purpose; we just forget it's in our hand. And he's honest about the limits. Marcus isn't describing grief, or serious anxiety, or anything a person should face rather than push down. Those need time, people, and sometimes a doctor. He means the everyday stuff: the stray irritation, the imagined argument, the small dread that floats in while you're doing the dishes. For those, the first move is to set them down and see if you even need to pick them back up. Often you don't. And when you do need to think it through, you can choose a better time than 2am.

564.title: Fit for you
564.hook: judge every word and act that fits you, and don't be swayed by blame (Meditations 5.3)
564.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.3 in two steps: first test an act for fairness and honesty, then, if it passes, don't let disapproval alone turn them aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was galene, the calm of a sea gone flat. Your line was a sea gone flat.

There's always someone with notes. You start eating differently and a relative comments. You speak up at a meeting and someone rolls their eyes. You give money to a cause and a friend calls it naive. Sometimes the critic is right, and it's worth listening. But often the right thing simply comes with a small crowd of people who'd rather you didn't. Marcus Aurelius, whose every public act had an audience, gave himself a rule for that crowd.
screen: `THERE'S ALWAYS SOMEONE WITH NOTES.` → `THE RIGHT THING HAS CRITICS.` → `FIT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Judge every word and act that is in line with nature, Marcus writes in book five, entry three, as fit for you. In Stoic terms, in line with nature means in line with what a reasoning, social creature is made for: honest, fair, useful to others. That's the test, and it comes first. Then: don't let the blame or the talk of certain people that follows turn you aside. If a thing is good to do or say, don't think it beneath you. Notice the order. Test the act first. If it passes, the critics don't get a vote. Those people, he says, have their own ruling mind and follow their own impulses. Don't keep looking over at them. That isn't contempt. Their mind is theirs to steer, and yours is yours. Go straight on, he finishes, following your own nature and the common nature, because the road of both is one. What's right for you, done honestly, is also right for the whole. This doesn't mean ignore all feedback. Elsewhere Marcus asks to be corrected, gladly, when he's wrong. A critic with a reason gets heard, and maybe changes your mind. A critic with only disapproval doesn't get to decide what's fit for you.

segments.voice: Think of one right thing you've held back from because of a critic, real or imagined, and test it honestly: is it fair, true, useful? If it fails, let it go. If it passes, let the critic keep their own mind, and picture yourself doing it calmly, without needing to win them over.

565.title: What is wholly yours
565.hook: they can't admire your cleverness, so show what's fully yours: sincerity, dignity, endurance (Meditations 5.5)
565.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes take one quality from the list in Meditations 5.5, such as sincerity, dignity or endurance, and practice it for a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus on what's fit for you; test the act, not the critics. Your line was fit for me.

Plenty of people have a sentence that starts, I'm just not. Not a math person. Not good at small talk. Not creative. Sometimes it's true, and sometimes it's a door we've closed so we don't have to try. A Roman emperor had one too. In his private notebook, the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius admits he isn't especially quick. Then, in book five, entry five, he turns that into a challenge.
screen: `I'M JUST NOT...` → `AN EMPEROR'S OWN SENTENCE.` → `WHAT IS WHOLLY YOURS.`

segments.voice: People can't admire your sharpness of mind, Marcus tells himself. Fine. Whether he was being modest or honest, we can't know, but he takes it as given. Then the turn: there are many other things where you can't claim, I'm not built for that. So show those, the ones entirely in your power: sincerity, dignity, endurance in hard work, not chasing pleasure, being content with what you have and with little, kindness, frankness, not loving excess, not chattering, a generous spirit. Not one of them needs talent. Do you see, he asks, how many of these you could show right now, with no excuse of being naturally unable? And yet you stay below the mark, by choice. Are you forced by your nature to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your body, to try to please people, to show off, to be restless in your mind? No. You could have been free of these long ago. And if you really are slower than others, he says, work at that too, and don't neglect it or enjoy being dull. Here's what makes this kind. Nothing on Marcus's list depends on gifts. A slow thinker can be sincere. A shy person can be kind. A tired person can refuse to grumble. Those are wholly yours.

566.title: Nature's prescription
566.hook: as doctors prescribe cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss; take it like medicine (Meditations 5.8)
566.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes reframe a hardship as in Meditations 5.8, accepting it as a doctor's order rather than resenting it only as bad luck.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, and what is wholly yours: sincerity, dignity, endurance. Your line was what is mine.

Physical therapy hurts. The stretch you're told to hold for thirty seconds feels like three minutes. The exercise for your knee is boring and sore. And yet people do it, more or less cheerfully, because someone they trust wrote it down and said: this will help. You don't argue with a prescription the way you argue with bad luck. Marcus Aurelius noticed that difference, and in book five, entry eight, he tried to move the hard things in his life from one column to the other.
screen: `PHYSICAL THERAPY HURTS.` → `YOU DON'T ARGUE WITH A PRESCRIPTION.` → `NATURE'S PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: People say, Marcus writes, Asclepius prescribed this man horseback riding, or cold baths, or walking barefoot. Asclepius was the Greek god of healing, and in Marcus's world people spoke of his prescriptions the way we speak of a doctor's orders. In the same way, he says, the nature of the whole prescribed for this person an illness, or a disability, or a loss. The word for prescribed is the same. In his view the event isn't random; it's fitted to you, the way a prescription is written for one patient. He gives two reasons to accept it. One: it happened to you, it was assigned to you, it's woven into your own life. Two: it serves the health of the whole universe, which he believed was one living order. You don't have to share his belief about the cosmos to feel the force of the first reason. This is your life, and this is in it. So, he says, accept what happens the way you accept what the doctor orders. Many prescriptions are bitter, and we welcome them anyway, hoping for health. You can't always choose whether hard things come. But you can choose their column: bad luck, to be resented, or medicine, to be taken. Marcus isn't saying it doesn't taste bitter. He's saying bitter isn't the same as wrong.

567.title: Back to it
567.hook: don't be disgusted when you fail; return, and be glad if most of what you do is decent (Meditations 5.9)
567.tomorrow: How am I using my soul?
567.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.9 after a lapse: no self-disgust, just a return to the practice, and contentment if most of their acts are decent.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nature's prescription, hard things taken as medicine. Your line was the prescription. And today the week closes.

A knitter drops a stitch three rows back. There are two ways this can go. In one, there's a sigh, a crochet hook, the stitch is picked up, and the scarf carries on. In the other, the whole thing is yanked off the needles in disgust and shoved in a drawer for a year. The dropped stitch is the same in both. The difference is the next minute. In book five, entry nine, Marcus Aurelius writes to himself about exactly that minute.

segments.voice: Don't be disgusted, discouraged or dissatisfied, Marcus tells himself, if you don't manage to do everything by right principles. He expects to fall short. A man who wrote this much about virtue knew how often he missed it. When you've been knocked off, he says, come back again. The whole practice is in that one word: not never fall, but return. And be content if the greater part of what you do is worthy of a human being. Not all of it. The greater part. Love the thing you're returning to. Then a lovely detail. Don't go back to philosophy as if to a schoolmaster with a cane, he says, but the way people with sore eyes go back to a sponge and egg, or someone goes back to a soothing bandage or a warm compress. Philosophy, for Marcus, is the medicine, not the punishment. You return because it helps. Now look at this week. Good fortune: luck is in the bearing. The gulf of time: a life against eternity. Push it away: set the troubling thought down. Fit for me: test the act, not the critics. What is mine: sincerity, dignity, endurance. The prescription: hard things as medicine. And now, back to it. You'll forget most of these lines by Thursday. That's fine. The practice was never to remember perfectly. It's to come back.

segments.voice: Think of one recent slip, and let the voice that comes with it, the disgust or the why bother, speak and pass. Then picture the next small step back into the habit, as if reaching for something soothing rather than something stern.
Marcus, who told himself not to be disgusted when he fell short, but to return, and be content if the greater part was worthy. Today's word.
Your line: a sponge and egg. Philosophy is the compress, not the cane. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and another week.
